topic: Permission, security, and privacy lifecycle: consent, revocation, least privilege, race handling, audit, and recovery
research_questions: What lifecycle controls do authoritative security and privacy standards require for consent, least privilege, revocation, race handling, auditability, and recovery?
How should a product model permission state, capability scope, expiry, revocation propagation, and recovery after denial or compromise?
Which platform patterns expose the user-visible and operator-visible evidence needed to prove permission transitions?
What unresolved risks remain when permission state changes concurrently with a tool or data operation?

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5.1: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.material_relevance: Provides the authoritative control vocabulary for consent and revocation of PII processing, least privilege, audit content and correlation, audit failure response, incident handling, and recovery to a known state.

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Authentication and Authenticator Management
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.material_relevance: Defines prompt authenticator invalidation after loss, compromise, or user request, session timeout and reauthentication expectations, and account-recovery binding and notification behavior.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
sources.material_relevance: Specifies least-privilege and audience restriction for access tokens, scope/resource binding for refresh tokens, replay defenses, rotation, expiration, and security-event revocation.

sources.title: RFC 7009: OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation
sources.material_relevance: Defines revocation of refresh and access tokens, cascading-grant considerations, client handling of unexpected invalidation, service-unavailable behavior, propagation delay, and revocation design trade-offs.

sources.title: RFC 7662: OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection
sources.material_relevance: Defines an authenticated state query exposing token activity, scope, subject, client, audience, issue and expiry metadata, and explicitly treats cache staleness as a revocation race risk.

sources.title: RFC 9396: OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests
sources.material_relevance: Provides structured authorization details for locations, actions, data types, identifiers, privileges, consent presentation, enrichment, and narrowed permissions.

sources.title: RFC 9449: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)
sources.material_relevance: Defines sender-constrained access and refresh tokens, key possession proofs, endpoint and method binding, and bounded proof replay windows for compromise recovery.

sources.title: Permissions
sources.material_relevance: Models browser permission state, permission-store keys, user-agent consent UI, expiry, queryability, change notification, and revocation behavior.

sources.title: Request runtime permissions
sources.material_relevance: Documents runtime, feature-specific permission requests, rationale and denial UX, asynchronous results, process termination on revocation, self-revocation, and automatic reset of unused permissions.

sources.title: Policy evaluation logic - AWS Identity and Access Management
sources.material_relevance: Shows how request context and multiple policy layers combine into effective access, including intersection boundaries and explicit-deny precedence.

sources.title: CloudTrail record contents for management, data, and network activity events
sources.material_relevance: Documents operator evidence fields for action, completion time, location, request parameters, responses, errors, and event-format limits.

sources.title: Auditing
sources.material_relevance: Provides a mature open-source pattern for chronological audit records, request execution stages, policy-selected metadata or bodies, and log or webhook backends.

findings.claim: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.1 supplies a customizable control framework rather than a universally self-executing law; when its controls are adopted and tailored, it covers authority to process PII, tailored and just-in-time consent, consent revocation, least privilege, time-correlated audit trails, audit failure response, incident handling, and recovery to a known state.
findings.notes: PT-2 limits processing to authorized purposes and calls for monitoring and auditing; the consent enhancements include tailored consent, just-in-time consent, and revocation. AC-6 states least privilege directly. AU controls cover audit content, time correlation, PII minimization, storage, failure response, and generation. CP-10 covers recovery and reconstitution. The organization-defined assignments mean implementation scope must be explicitly selected and documented.

findings.claim: NIST SP 800-63B treats invalidation, session termination, reauthentication, and account recovery as distinct lifecycle controls: authenticators must be promptly invalidated after compromise, loss, or a subscriber request; sessions have overall and inactivity limits; recovery binds new authenticators and sends notifications.
findings.notes: The guidance also warns that an access token and refresh tokens can remain valid after the authentication session ends, so session presence cannot stand in for current authorization.

findings.claim: The OAuth security lifecycle is lease-like and layered: privileges should be restricted to the minimum required and an intended audience; refresh tokens must remain bound to consented scope and resources; public clients need sender constraint or rotation; and revocation can be triggered by logout, password change, or a security event.
findings.notes: RFC 7009 defines a revocation endpoint and cascade behavior while requiring clients to tolerate unexpected invalidation. RFC 9700 and RFC 9449 add rotation, sender-constrained tokens, and proof-of-possession defenses for compromise and replay.

findings.claim: A permission request should be represented as structured authorization details, not only a boolean: RFC 9396 provides fields for resource locations, actions, data types, identifiers, and privileges, and expects the authorization server to decide how those details are shown, enriched, or narrowed during consent.
findings.notes: The same specification allows a refreshed token to carry fewer permissions without changing the resource owner's earlier grant, which supports modeling current capability separately from historical consent.

findings.claim: An effective authorization decision needs current-state checks for activity, expiration, not-before, revocation, signature, and resource-server audience; token introspection can expose this state, but caching creates an explicit stale-authorization window.
findings.notes: RFC 7662 requires applicable state checks and describes the trade-off between short cache lifetimes, load, and stale revoked-token use. RFC 7009 separately describes propagation delay between servers.

findings.claim: The W3C Permissions model exposes a user-agent permission store keyed by a permission descriptor and context, with prompt, granted, and denied states; applications can query state, observe changes, and must react when the user revokes permission, while the user agent retains control through UI, preferences, and expiry policy.
findings.notes: This supplies a concrete user-visible and application-observable state pattern, but it does not define a server-side authorization transaction or an operator audit record.

findings.claim: Android's runtime permission pattern combines feature-specific requests, an explanatory rationale, a user-controlled system dialog, an asynchronous result, and an explicit denied path; revocation can terminate the app process, self-revocation is asynchronous, and unused permissions can be auto-reset.
findings.notes: The documented pattern makes denial a supported product state rather than an exception and requires the app to re-check permission before using the protected API.

findings.claim: AWS IAM demonstrates that effective permission is a composition of request context and policy layers rather than a single stored grant: boundaries and organization policies can intersect with identity and resource policies, and an explicit deny overrides an allow.
findings.notes: A product model should preserve the contributing policy layers and the decision reason if operators need to explain why access was denied or later changed.

findings.claim: Operator-visible proof is strongest when it records both decision context and lifecycle stage: CloudTrail records action, completion time, request location, request parameters, responses, and errors; Kubernetes audit records can be chronological, staged at receipt and completion, and selected at metadata, request, or request-response levels.
findings.notes: Kubernetes requires an audit policy for records to be emitted, and both ecosystems expose configuration and payload-size or privacy trade-offs.

findings.claim: The reviewed standards establish propagation-delay and stale-cache risks but do not define a universal atomic linearization point between permission revocation and a concurrent tool or data operation.
findings.notes: This is a bounded absence claim about the reviewed source set, not proof that no other standard addresses the problem. RFC 7009 leaves propagation windows to system design and risk analysis; RFC 7662 makes cache freshness a deployment trade-off.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Represent consent as typed, resource-scoped authorization details that name the action, data type, resource location or identifier, privilege, and any narrowed or enriched values shown during consent.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A permission UI and audit record can prove exactly what was requested and granted instead of recording only an allow/deny bit.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Use short-lived, audience-restricted capabilities with explicit revocation, refresh-token rotation or sender constraint, and risk-based expiry.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Compromise recovery can reduce both the number of usable descendants and the time they remain usable, while preserving a clear revocation boundary.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Expose current capability state through an authenticated introspection path that reports activity, scope, subject, client, audience, and time bounds, with deliberately bounded caching.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A resource server can make decisions from current authorization state, but the product must make cache age and stale-use risk explicit.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Keep a context-keyed permission store with prompt, granted, and denied states, a query API, change notification, user-controlled revocation, and optional expiry.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: The user-facing surface can show current state and react to revocation without treating a prior approval as permanent.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Request access at the point a feature needs it, explain the feature-specific reason, handle an asynchronous user decision, and re-check or terminate protected work when the operating system revokes access.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Denial, revocation, auto-reset, and re-prompt become normal state transitions that the product can expose rather than hidden exceptions.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Evaluate effective access from multiple policy layers with explicit deny precedence, then emit a chronological audit trail that identifies actor, action, target, timing, result, and request lifecycle stage.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Operators can reconstruct both why a decision was made and whether the protected operation was merely received, started, completed, or failed.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A revocation is accepted by the authority while one or more resource servers still accept the capability during propagation.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Represent revocation as an event with a measurable propagation deadline, fan it out to enforcement points, prefer stateful handles or short-lived access tokens for high-risk operations, and define what happens while the deadline is not met.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A protected resource authorizes from a cached active result after the token or grant has been revoked.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Set cache lifetime from data sensitivity and revocation likelihood, disable caching for the most sensitive effects, and attach cache age to the authorization evidence.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A stolen bearer or refresh token is replayed before revocation or used to mint additional capabilities.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use sender-constrained tokens or rotation, bind refresh tokens to scope and resources, keep access tokens short-lived, detect replay, revoke the grant and descendants, and force a fresh recovery path.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A permission check succeeds, the permission changes, and a tool or data operation applies the stale decision.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use a transaction or compare-and-swap authorization fence that binds the decision version to the side effect; otherwise treat the boundary as an unresolved TOCTOU risk.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A grant that is recorded as a broad scope or role permits more resources, actions, data types, or audiences than the user understood.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Represent the capability with structured resource, action, data-type, identifier, privilege, and audience constraints; evaluate the intersection at use time and display the effective set during consent.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A long-running stream, background job, or queued tool call continues after the user or operator revokes its authority.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Define revocation checkpoints for admission, each sensitive side effect, and commit; cancel or quarantine work that fails the fence, and record partial effects for compensation or review.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Audit evidence is missing, truncated, delayed, or itself exposes more personal data or token material than the investigation requires.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Minimize payloads and PII, protect logs separately, correlate timestamps and event IDs, monitor audit pipeline failures, document truncation, and preserve a durable decision digest when full bodies are not retained.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A denial or compromise is followed by an overly easy regrant that restores the same compromised session, key, or queued capability.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Separate denial from recovery, invalidate the old authenticator and descendants, notify the subscriber, require a risk-appropriate recovery method, and bind new capabilities to a new session or key.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The user interface says a permission is revoked or denied while an operator view or enforcement point still reflects a prior state, or vice versa.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Publish a shared transition ID, authorization revision, effective time, propagation status, and last observed enforcement state to both projections; do not present a local UI write as globally effective until confirmed.

implications.implication: Permission state should be modeled as a versioned grant or capability record, not a boolean flag.
implications.rationale: The sources distinguish context, resource, action, data type, subject, audience, expiry, active state, and revocation. A boolean cannot preserve enough information to explain or safely re-evaluate a transition.

implications.implication: The effective capability should be the intersection of subject identity, consented scope, resource and action constraints, audience, policy layers, session state, expiry, and revocation status.
implications.rationale: AWS documents policy intersections and explicit denies; OAuth documents minimum privilege, audience, scope, and current token checks. Combining them yields a safer cross-layer model than trusting one grant source.

implications.implication: A successful authorization decision must carry a freshness or revision boundary into the tool or data operation that produces the side effect.
implications.rationale: The standards expose propagation and cache windows, while staged audit records distinguish request receipt from completion. The product must connect those boundaries if it needs a meaningful answer to whether revocation preceded the effect.

implications.implication: Recovery after denial, loss, or compromise should be modeled as a new lifecycle with notifications, reauthentication or reproofing, new binding, and explicit invalidation of old descendants.
implications.rationale: NIST defines recovery and notifications; OAuth defines security-event revocation, rotation, and sender constraint. A simple retry of the old session would bypass those controls.

implications.implication: Each permission transition needs a user-readable explanation and an operator-grade evidence record linked by a shared transition identity, while both surfaces minimize privacy-sensitive content.
implications.rationale: The user agent exposes state and change behavior; NIST requires useful but privacy-limited audit content; CloudTrail and Kubernetes show concrete operator event fields and stages.

implications.implication: Unavailable revocation or introspection evidence, audit pipeline failure, and stale state need an explicit risk policy rather than an implicit allow.
implications.rationale: RFC 7009 treats a service-unavailable response as evidence the token may still exist; RFC 7662 frames cache freshness as a security trade-off; NIST requires response to audit logging failure.

novel_ideas.idea: Issue each capability as a versioned authorization lease containing grant revision, subject, resource, action, data type, audience, expiry, and key binding; revocation increments the grant revision and enforcement rejects older revisions.
novel_ideas.rationale: Structured authorization details supply the scope dimensions; introspection supplies current state; OAuth BCP and DPoP supply expiry, audience, rotation, and sender binding. A revision fence adds a product-level way to close propagation and TOCTOU gaps.

novel_ideas.idea: Create a transition receipt for every grant, denial, expiry, revocation, or recovery event with a transition ID, prior and next state, actor, reason, effective time, authorization revision, affected descendants, and propagation observations; render a redacted version to the user and a detailed version to operators.
novel_ideas.rationale: The sources provide the ingredients for state change, time correlation, actor/action context, staged observation, and privacy minimization, but do not prescribe one cross-surface receipt.

novel_ideas.idea: Attach the authorization revision to every queued tool call, stream, batch item, and worker lease; revalidate the revision immediately before each sensitive side effect and at final commit, with quarantine and compensation paths for failures.
novel_ideas.rationale: Propagation delay and staged request completion make a one-time check insufficient for long-lived work. The fence turns the unresolved race into an explicit admission and commit policy.

novel_ideas.idea: Define an uncertainty envelope for stale, unavailable, or failed permission evidence: allow only low-risk reads under a bounded age, queue or deny high-risk effects, surface the reason to the user, and create an audit event for the uncertainty decision.
novel_ideas.rationale: The standards expose explicit unavailability, stale-cache, and audit-failure conditions. A named envelope prevents each product component from inventing a different fail-open behavior.

novel_ideas.idea: Store the authorization decision as a compact graph of contributing grant, policy layers, explicit denies, token state, audience, and freshness, then project a plain-language explanation to users and a machine-readable trace to operators.
novel_ideas.rationale: AWS policy composition, OAuth current-state claims, and NIST audit-content controls imply that the explanation must preserve both the positive and negative inputs without storing raw secrets or unnecessary PII.

novel_ideas.idea: On suspected compromise, move the grant into quarantine: revoke descendants, reject queued work with the old revision, require risk-appropriate recovery and new key binding, notify the subscriber, and retain a redacted transition receipt for review.
novel_ideas.rationale: NIST recovery requires notifications and new authenticator binding; OAuth requires or recommends revocation, rotation, and sender constraint. Quarantine extends those controls to asynchronous product work.

unresolved_questions.question: What consistency guarantee does the product promise when a permission revocation and a tool or data side effect are concurrent: immediate linearizability, bounded staleness, cancellation, or compensation after completion?
Which reads, writes, streams, background jobs, and external tool calls are cancellable after revocation, and which require a compensating action or an operator review?
What maximum revocation propagation time is acceptable per capability class, and how is that bound measured across all enforcement points and caches?
What minimum evidence lets a user and an operator prove a permission transition without exposing raw tokens, sensitive request bodies, or unnecessary personal data?
How should a denial on one device or surface interact with a legitimate regrant on another device, while ensuring that a compromised session or key cannot silently regain the old capability?

If the audit pipeline is unavailable, full, delayed, or configured to omit request and response bodies, what durable proof is retained before a permission transition or protected operation is allowed to complete?
